extracted.intended_audience: military legal officers, Judge Advocate General's Office, War Department counsel, government attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Digest of Judge Advocate General and War Department opinions summarizing legal standards governing the National Guard/Navy Militia (District of Columbia and States) and federal regulation of navigable waters (bridges, structures, harbor lines, obstructions). Useful for legal-administrative decisionmaking about property, pay, equipment, jurisdiction, and permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: No reduction of leave time or pay while so employed
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that the commanding general of the National Guard of the District of Columbia should not be charged against any time due them in the operation of the laws granting leaves of absence, and that there should be no reduction of pay for absence while so employed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniforms and campaign badge entitlement for National Guard of D.C.
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that the uniform of the National Guard of the District of Columbia shall be the same as prescribed and furnished to the Army of the United States; officers of the Organized Militia of the District are entitled to receive campaign badges under the same conditions as Army officers; badges for enlisted men may lawfully be included in issues, but badges for commissioned officers should be obtained by purchase; the badge cannot be withheld from an enlisted man of the National Guard who had served honorably during the Philippine campaign; the commanding general is competent to determine when an officer has rendered service entitling him to wear the distinctive campaign badge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies the Army's distribution rules to the District Guard; distinguishes issued enlisted badges from officer procurement; places determination authority with commanding general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoppage of volunteer pay and reporting for failure to account for US property
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that where a militia officer (later volunteer) failed to account for certain U.S. property, the commanding general recommended stoppage of his pay as a volunteer to make good the failure; the Secretary of War may suspend payment of volunteer pay pending prompt action by the commanding general under the militia act; if a judgment is obtained which cannot be satisfied, it should be promptly reported to the Secretary of War for action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connects administrative pay stoppage to property accountability actions and requires reporting unsatisfied judgments to War Dept for further action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commanding general remains responsible for U.S. property in militia possession unless formally relieved
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that in the meantime the commanding general of the District Militia must continue solely responsible to the United States for all U.S. property in the possession of such militia unless regularly relieved from such responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure depending on location of property when officer denies receipt
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that if under the militia act the officer had any property within the District, the District Militia authorities could proceed against it, and if he had none within the jurisdiction the action could await his return; and that the War Department could not, merely because the officer denied having received the property, grant permission to drop the United States property from returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not remove items from official returns based on officer denial alone; jurisdictional proceedings depend on presence of property within District.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property-accountability evidence standards assimilated to Regular Army; use of certificates
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that because the system of property accountability in the National Guard of the District is closely assimilated to that prevailing in the Regular Army, the same or similar rules of evidence should apply in determining property-responsibility questions, and officers may lawfully be permitted to give testimony in the form of certificates similar to those required of Regular Army officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher standards of performance/evidence than typical state law may be required; permits analogous certificate-based testimony for militia officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Armament, clothing, equipment, subsistence and consumables remain governed by sections 31 and 57
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that subsequent legislation does not annul or invalidate the requirement of section 31 (armament, clothing, equipment) or section 57 (during encampment or when ordered to aid civil authorities regulates subsistence) of the act of March 1, 1889; forage and fuel can be furnished while in camp; 'consumable property' remains U.S. property until actually consumed; specified military manuals (e.g., Dyer's Handbook) may be issued as 'other military stores' necessary for training; blank administrative forms may be furnished under section 55.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms continuing federal obligations and property ownership rules for consumables and supplies issued to militia during authorized activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility to share in 'two-million-dollar' clause benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that the Organized Militia of the District of Columbia is entitled to share in the benefits conferred by the 'two million dollar' clause of the act of March 2, 1903, and the cost of supplies can be charged against the District's allotment under that act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enables charging certain supply costs to congressional allotment provided for militia support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issuance and funding of typewriting machines to militia
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that War Department orders prescribing kinds of typewriters for Army purchase do not prohibit the Quartermaster's Department from issuing and charging to the Militia of the District a typewriting machine of a different make on hand; typewriting machines may be issued to the National Guard of the District to the same extent as corresponding Regular Army organizations and their cost will constitute a charge against the District allotment under section 1661.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quartermaster discretion allowed to issue existing equipment to militia; cost treatment parallels Regular Army issuance rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Furniture for District National Guard must be funded from special appropriation item for 'furniture'
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that the cost of requested furniture cannot be charged to the general appropriation for arming and equipping the militia (act of June 6, 1900), but must be met by the special annual appropriation which includes an item for 'furniture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes appropriate funding sources; furniture is not chargeable to broad equipment appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War lacks authority to direct commanding general to loan U.S. property
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that the Secretary of War has no authority to direct the commanding general, District Militia, to loan property of the United States in his custody (e.g., horse equipments for parade use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custodial control by commanding general cannot be overridden by Secretary to compel loans of U.S. property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loans of equipment (e.g., two-mule team) to militia may be improper under appropriation law
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that while a loan of a two-mule team with wagon for rifle practice might be authorized in spirit of the militia act, it becomes of doubtful propriety when considered in connection with restrictive provisions of the Army support appropriation and the separate provision for incidental expenses of the National Guard in the District government appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriation limitations may bar or render questionable loans even if substantively useful for militia activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: No appeal from discharge by commanding general of District Militia
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that there is no appeal from a discharge by the commanding general of the District Militia, and that such a discharge cannot be recalled or set aside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative discharge decisions by commanding general are final under the cited authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality of executed court-martial dishonorable discharge
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that where an enlisted man was dishonorably discharged pursuant to an approved court-martial sentence and the sentence executed, a request to substitute an honorable discharge for the dishonorable one cannot be afforded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court-martial sentences, once executed, cannot be administratively converted to more favorable characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications and effects of inclusion on list of eligibles under Jan 21, 1903 (section 23)
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that section 23 provides examinations of persons with specific qualifications (served in Regular Army, volunteer forces, Organized Militia, or attended U.S. military schools); the statute's purpose is to secure a list of persons specially qualified to hold commissions in any future volunteer force and should be liberally construed; Organized Militia members are proper candidates; entry on the list of eligibles does not confer military rank; current Army appropriations apply to paying eligibles who attend military schools, with same allowances as provided for Organized Militia officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry on eligibility list is administratively significant (for future commissions and schooling allowances) but confers no rank; liberal construction favored to populate eligibles.

rubrics_metrics.name: War Department has no statutory authority over Naval Militia; funding and supply provided by Navy appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that no legislation of Congress imposes duties upon the War Department in connection with the Naval Militia, arms for its use are provided in naval appropriations, and furnishing small arms for Naval Militia would be a charge against the Navy appropriation; War Department has no statutory relations with Naval Militia and is without authority to sell stores to a State for the use of its Naval Militia or to exchange Navy-issued arms for War Department arms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draws a clear administrative-appropriations and jurisdictional line between War and Navy Departments regarding Naval Militia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naval Militia excluded from certain Army-oriented competitions and provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that the Naval Militia is not among the forces entitled to participate in national competitions provided for in the act of April 23, 1904, and should be excluded from competitions and benefits limited to forces expressly named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion in statutory competitions/benefits depends on express mention in enactments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay entitlement for naval battalion practice cruises and maneuvers (limited/fund-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Held in part that the naval battalion National Guard engaged in a practice cruise was not entitled to payment under some Army provisions (Secretary of War did not concur that War Dept could pay certain expenses), but also held that the battalion was entitled to pay out of monies appropriated by Congress for the District in the act of March 2, 1907, which specifically provided for practice cruises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entitlement to pay depends on the statutory source—Army maneuver statutes may not cover Naval Militia, but specific District appropriations can authorize pay for practice cruises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia service not 'service in the Armies of the United States' for naturalization statute
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that an honorable discharge from the Organized Militia does not constitute service 'in the Armies of the United States, with the Regular or Volunteer forces' within the meaning of the naturalization statute (section 2166, R.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Militia service generally does not substitute for federal Army service in immigration/naturalization contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War may furnish transcript of regimental history to State governors under March 2, 1895, but scope limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that the act authorizes the Secretary to furnish a transcript of the history of any regiment or company 'of his State' at State expense; it applies to State troops organized by States to enter as volunteers and to Organized Militia of States mustered into U.S. service, but not to organizations that are distinctively United States organizations with which States had nothing to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility to obtain transcripts is tied to whether the unit is a State-organized unit or a purely U.S. organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge Advocate General's role regarding State militia laws—advice limited to sufficiency for federal statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Held, that purely State matters relative to the State militia should be settled in the State; the propriety of the War Department passing on sufficiency of a State law to meet conditions of section 3 of the act of January 21, 1903, is doubtful; however, upon presentation of a contemplated militia law for a State with request for information as to its sufficiency, the Judge Advocate General may advise as to the sufficiency for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JAG may provide advisory opinions on whether proposed State militia laws satisfy federally-stated requisites, but generally should avoid intervening in purely State administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal regulation of bridges and structures over navigable waters—Secretary of War powers and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Held (legislative and interpretive summary): under acts from 1884, 1888, 1890 and consolidated by the Rivers and Harbors Act of March 3, 1899, the Secretary of War has authority to require persons or corporations owning/operating a bridge that is an obstruction to navigation to provide aids, to alter or remove obstructions to render navigation free and unobstructed, and to approve location and plans before construction; failure to comply can trigger fines and penalties; deposit of refuse and erection of structures without permission is prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places preconstruction-plan-approval, alteration and removal obligations on bridge/structure owners; administrative notice and opportunity to be heard are required before orders; penalties for noncompliance are statutory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of key sections of Rivers and Harbors legislation (sections 9–15 enumerated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Synopsis: section 9 relates to bridges, dams or causeways; section 10 to other structures and excavating/filling; section 11 to establishment of harbor lines; section 12 prescribes penalties for violations of sections 9–11; section 13 prohibits deposit of refuse matter injuring navigation; section 14 forbids injury to works for improvement of navigation; section 15 relates to (text continues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the statutory map for enforcement, permitting, penalties, and harbor-line regulation under federal navigable-waters law.
